subject: zoology
question_text: What are the salient features of the echinoids?

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack zoology section (book p.36, SAQ 27). Zoology holds only ONE source book — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only, and no zoology board paper is in the corpus — so the two-book union check and the back-test are both structurally impossible for this card; 'not checked' does NOT mean 'checked and clean'. The mark split is a claim until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. BOOK SPELLING corrected here: the book prints 'Peidicellaria' for pedicellariae and 'calcarious' for calcareous.

steps.label: What the echinoids are
steps.why: The class is defined by what it does not have — no arms — which is why the body closes into a globe or a disc instead of spreading into a star.
common_mistakes: Giving them arms. Arms are absent in Echinoidea; it is the starfish that has arms.
Calling Echinoidea a phylum. It is a class of the phylum Echinodermata.
steps.memory_tip: Echinoid means spiny and globular: a ball or a disc, with no arms.
steps.margin_note: Class, phylum, body form, and the absence of arms. Four or five lines.
lines: Echinoidea is a class of the phylum
Its members are the sea urchins, the heart
The body form is semi-globular or disc-like.

steps.label: Test, spines and pedicellariae
steps.why: The ossicles are locked together instead of lying loose in the skin, and that fixed test is what gives the spines a firm base to be worked from.
common_mistakes: Writing that the spines are fixed. In echinoids the spines are movable.
Giving the pedicellariae five jaws. A pedicellaria has three jaws; Aristotle's lantern has five.
steps.memory_tip: Three jaws for a pedicellaria, five jaws for the lantern. Keep the two counts apart.
steps.margin_note: Test, spines, pedicellariae, grooves. Four short lines.
lines: The calcareous ossicles are united to form a
strong shell called the test, or corona.
The spines over the body are movable.

steps.label: Aristotle's lantern
steps.why: The mouth faces the rock the animal feeds on and the anus faces away from it, so the two openings lie on opposite surfaces of the test.
common_mistakes: Placing the anus on the oral surface. In echinoids the anus is aboral.
Writing that every echinoid has the lantern. It is absent in the heart urchin.
steps.memory_tip: Mouth below on the rock, anus above. The lantern is the five-jawed mill at the mouth.
steps.margin_note: Position of the two openings, then the lantern. The five jaws carry the mark.

steps.label: Larva and examples
steps.why: The larva is named after the class it belongs to, so echinopluteus goes with Echinoidea just as auricularia goes with Holothuroidea.
common_mistakes: Naming the bipinnaria. That is the larva of a starfish; the echinoid larva is the echinopluteus.
Giving no example. Two or three named animals are expected.
steps.memory_tip: Echinopluteus for the echinoid, and all three examples begin with Echino-.
steps.margin_note: Larva in one line, then the examples. Close with the boxed hallmarks.

insider_note: Aristotle's lantern is asked as a 2-mark question of its own, so it is always worth a full line here — five jaws, in the buccal cavity of the sea urchin.
